title: Functional overreaching: the key to peak performance during the taper?
authors: Aubry A, Hausswirth C, Louis J, Coutts AJ, Le Meur Y
journal: Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise
findings: 33 trained male triathletes were assigned to overload training (n=23) or normal training (n=10, CTL) for 8 weeks, with 3-week overload and 4-week taper; 11 of 23 were diagnosed functionally overreached (F-OR, decreased performance with high perceived fatigue) and 12 were only acutely fatigued (AF).
By qualitative statistics the AF group showed a small to large greater peak performance supercompensation than the F-OR group (2.6% +/- 1.1%) and the CTL group (2.6% +/- 1.6%).
60%, 83% and 73% of peak performances occurred within the first two weeks of taper in CTL, AF and OR groups respectively.

Ten infections were reported, with higher prevalence in F-OR (70%) than AF (20%) and CTL (10%); authors conclude peak performance is not delayed when heavy training immediately precedes the taper, and F-OR carries a higher risk of maladaptation including infection.
limitations: Male triathletes, cycling outcome, not runners; qualitative statistics; subgroups (F-OR vs AF) defined post hoc, 11-12 per group; assignment method to overload vs normal not stated.
implications: Peak performance mostly arrives in the first two taper weeks, which supports not extending the taper beyond about 3 weeks (extrapolation; the study itself used a 4-week taper).

Avoid scheduling a large overload block immediately before the taper without monitoring; if the athlete shows functional overreaching signs (performance drop with high perceived fatigue) at taper start, do not add load and flag higher illness risk. The study did not test whether a longer taper helps F-OR athletes, so no taper extension is justified from it.
Infection risk was 70% in the overreached subgroup; flag illness prevention and monitoring after heavy pre-taper load.

verification.notes: Crossref returns short title 'Functional Overreaching' (MSSE Sep 2014, Aubry first author). Design changed rct to other and level B to C (assignment not described as randomized; post hoc subgrouping). Researcher's 'extend the taper' advice was not supported and was removed.
